source.title_on_document: The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking

supplement.where: Referred to as 'supplementary material' (p. 4, Section 3.1); no URL given. The PDF holds only Appendix A (NASA-TLX means, p. 18).
supplement.holds: The full study protocol. All outcome statistics (Tables 1-4, Figures 6-9) are in the main text.

paper_design_summary: Sixty university students with visual-design experience were randomly assigned (20 per condition) to sketch as many ideas as possible for a chatbot avatar in 20 minutes, after seeing an example robot avatar meant to induce fixation, with no inspiration support, Google Image Search, or Midjourney V4. The sketches were scored for design fixation (features copied from the example, counted by two blind raters), fluency (number of sketches), variety (number of rater-made idea clusters a participant's sketches fall into), and originality (share of other participants without an idea in the same cluster), and analyzed with Bayesian models.

studies.label: Lab experiment: chatbot-avatar sketching with no support, Google Image Search, or Midjourney

assignment.what_was_assigned: Inspiration Stimulus available during the 20-minute sketching task: none (Baseline), Google Image Search, or Midjourney V4 (GenAI).
assignment.quote: After completing the questionnaire, the participants were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions and were assigned a unique ID generated by the computer (3 random digits)
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 3.3 Procedure; design described as between-participants on p. 3, Section 3 and p. 4, Section 3.1

arms.name: Baseline (No support)
arms.description: No inspiration support; sketching on paper from the written brief and the example avatar.

arms.name: Image Search
arms.description: Access to Google Images in an incognito browser during the task.

arms.name: GenAI
arms.description: Access to the paid Midjourney V4 through a private Discord server; text prompts return sets of four images.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper gives 60 participants and 20 per condition (10 women and 10 men each). The NASA-TLX ANOVA is reported as F(2, 57), consistent with 60 people. The paper does not state the number of rows in each outcome model.
participants.who: Undergraduate, master's, and PhD students from arts, business, computer science and IT, design, engineering, and science, aged 18 or older with self-described visual-design experience; mean age 25.8 (range 18-49, SD 5.4). Recruited through university student notice boards, student-club mailing lists, and word of mouth. Few had professional industry experience (p. 16).
participants.quote: We recruited 60 participants through digital student notice boards, mailing lists of university student clubs, and word of mouth.

ai_tool.name_model: Midjourney V4 (paid version, default model in May 2023), via a private Discord server
ai_tool.how_used: Participants typed text prompts to generate sets of four images and used them as inspiration while sketching ideas on paper. Participants created 117 prompts in total (mean 5.85 per participant, median 5.5, range 2-15) (p. 11).

task.description: Sketch as many ideas as possible for an avatar for a 'kind, loving, caring, and intelligent' chatbot, on paper, after being shown an example robot avatar with 14 salient features (Figure 1) to induce design fixation.
task.duration: 20-minute design task within a 45-60 minute session

outcomes.name: Design fixation score (DFS)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two raters blind to the experiment's aims counted the presence of the 14 salient features of the example avatar in each sketch; DFS = features repeated / 14. Raters were HCI researchers with experience in teaching and evaluating design (p. 7, Section 3.4). The paper says inter-rater reliability was computed but prints no value (p. 5). Higher DFS = more copying of the example (worse). Modeled as binomial (N = 14) with probit link and random effects for participant and image (Table 1).

contrasts.reported: Table 1 (probit, posterior mean (posterior SD) [89% CI]): GenAI .32 (0.13) [.11, .54]; Intercept -.71 (.10) [-.86, .56] as printed. Text: 'mean = .32, 89% CI [.11, .55]', 100% probability of higher DFS, Bayes Factor 124. Arm-level posterior predictions shown only in Figure 6. Higher DFS means more fixation.

No direct GenAI-vs-Image-Search estimate. Both vs Baseline in Table 1: GenAI .32 (0.13) [.11, .54]; Image Search .27 (0.14) [.05, .48] (text: [.05, .49], 98% probability, BF 42.48). Text: 'GenAI led to even more design fixation than Image Search'.

outcomes.name: Fluency (number of sketches)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of sketches each participant produced in 20 minutes. Negative binomial, log link. Total-effects model: Fluency ~ Stimulus. Direct-effects model adds offset(log(Time on Task)).

contrasts.reported: Table 2 (log scale, posterior mean (SD) [89% CI]): total effect GenAI -.21 (.30) [-.66, .26]; direct effect GenAI .10 (.31) [-.39, .58]. Text: total -.21, 89% CI [-.7, .28], BF 3.20, 76% probability negative; direct .10, 89% CI [-.41, .60], BF .61, 38% probability negative. Arm-level predictions only in Figure 7.

No direct GenAI-vs-Image-Search estimate. Total effects vs Baseline (Table 2): GenAI -.21 (.30) [-.66, .26]; Image Search -.49 (.25) [-.88, -.10] (text: [-.9, -.10], BF 46.62, 98% probability negative).

outcomes.name: Variety (share of idea clusters a participant's sketches cover)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two raters blind to conditions grouped all 277 sketches into 83 mutually exclusive clusters (appearance, embodiment, appendages, shape, accessories). Variety = (clusters a participant's sketches fall in - 1) / (83 - 1). Negative binomial, log link, on the count of clusters minus one. Total-effects model: Variety ~ Stimulus. Direct-effects model adds Fluency.

contrasts.reported: Table 3 (log scale, posterior mean (SD) [89% CI]): total effect GenAI -.29 (-.28) [-.74, .17] (SD printed as negative); direct effect GenAI -.15 (0.24) [-.53, .23]. Text: total -.29, 89% CI [-.75, .16], 86% probability negative, BF 5.93; direct -.15 [-55, .24] as printed, BF 2.64. Arm-level predictions only in Figure 8.
No direct GenAI-vs-Image-Search estimate. Total effects vs Baseline (Table 3): GenAI -.29 (-.28) [-.74, .17]; Image Search -.39 (.28) [-.84, -.06] (text: -.40, [-.87, -.07], BF 11.38).

outcomes.name: Originality (cluster rarity of each sketch)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Originality = 1 - (number of other participants with ideas in the sketch's cluster / number of other participants), using the 83 rater-made clusters built from all 277 sketches. The paper does not say whether 'other participants' is restricted to the same condition. Linear regression with a participant random effect; total model Originality ~ Stimulus + (1|Participant ID), direct model adds Variety. Figure 9 shows values averaged per participant.

contrasts.reported: Table 4 (posterior mean (SD) [89% CI]): total effect GenAI -.03 (.02) [-.06, -.01]; direct effect GenAI -.03 (0.02) [-.05, -.01]; Intercept .86 (.01) total. Text: total -.03, 89% CI [-.06, .00], 97% probability negative, BF 35. Arm-level predictions only in Figure 9.
No direct GenAI-vs-Image-Search estimate. Total effects vs Baseline (Table 4): GenAI -.03 (.02) [-.06, -.01]; Image Search -.01 (.02) [-.04, .01] (text: BF 3.9).

company_involvement.description: Funded by the Rowden White Scholarship and the Melbourne Research Scholarship (University of Melbourne). No company role stated.

eligibility.reason: Participants were randomly assigned to Midjourney, Google Image Search, or no support (p. 6). The study has 60 people across all arms (p. 5), just above the 50 threshold; the GenAI-vs-Baseline contrast alone has 40 people (20 per arm). Outcomes are scored on the sketches by blind raters and cluster counts (pp. 5, 8-10).

one_line_finding: With Midjourney available, students copied more features of the example avatar (design fixation probit coefficient .32, 89% CI [.11, .54]) and produced sketches of lower originality (-.03, [-.06, -.01]) than with no support, with weaker negative estimates for fluency (-.21, [-.66, .26]) and variety (-.29, [-.74, .17]) (pp. 8-10, Tables 1-4).
open_questions: Equal arms of 20 with 10 women and 10 men per condition suggest blocked or stratified assignment, but the paper describes only random assignment with a computer-generated ID (p. 6).
Whether originality counts other participants across all three conditions or within the participant's own condition is not stated (p. 5, Eq. 4).
The row count of the sketch-level models (Tables 1 and 4) is not printed; 277 is the total sketch count from p. 5.
notes: No outcome measures similarity across different people's outputs, so no across_people outcome is recorded; originality is a per-sketch rarity score against the pooled sketches. All estimates are Bayesian (brms) posterior means with posterior SDs, 89% compatibility intervals, and Bayes factors; no arm means, SDs, or p-values are printed, and arm-level posterior predictions appear only in Figures 6-9. Section 3 names the four measures as 'the dependent variables', so all four are marked paper_primary; no single primary is named. Text and tables disagree slightly on several intervals (e.g., fluency GenAI total [-.7, .28] in text vs [-.66, .26] in Table 2; variety GenAI direct printed as [-55, .24] in text; originality GenAI total [-.06, .00] in text vs [-.06, -.01] in Table 4; Table 1 intercept interval printed as [-.86, .56]; Table 3 GenAI total SD printed as (-.28)). Not listed as outcomes: Spearman correlation between sketch DFS and the DFS of the preceding Midjourney images within the GenAI arm (rho = 0.56, 82 of 92 GenAI sketches, p. 12, Figure 10), a mechanism analysis with no comparison arm; the share of AI images that were humanoid robots (206/468, p. 12); NASA-TLX workload, self-reported (F(2,57) = 1, p = 0.37, p. 6; Appendix Table A.1); and qualitative interview themes.
